reading.title: Sharpening the Weather Report
reading.purpose: Watch a student revise a morning forecast by swapping vague words for exact ones.
paras: Owen handed his script to his older sister Clara across the kitchen table. "I read the morning forecast on the school intercom tomorrow," he said. "Be honest—how does it sound so far?"
Clara skimmed the page and smiled. "Do you want the gentle version or the blunt version?" Owen laughed. "Give me the direct truth. I want the whole school to actually know what to wear."

Clara tapped line one with her pen. "Writing that the weather will be bad is way too vague because listeners cannot tell whether to grab umbrellas or winter coats." She underlined the date. "Give them specific details, like the exact temperature and when rain begins."

"Fair point," Owen said, crossing out the line. "What about the second paragraph?" Clara raised an eyebrow. "It is super verbose—you used thirty-four words just to say a storm is coming. Intercom time is short, so keep your sentences concise while still being thorough enough to cover morning, lunch, and dismissal."

Owen grinned and began revising on a fresh card. "How about this: expect a faint mist at sunrise, weak enough to fade by eight o'clock, followed by a mild breeze and sixty-two degrees at recess. No intense downpours today—just moderate showers after three, neither a drizzle nor a flood."
Clara gave him a thumbs-up. "Now that sounds like a real weather desk report. Every word earns its spot on the page, and nobody will get caught in the rain."

qs.q: In paragraph 4, the word "verbose" most nearly means
choices: missing important facts about afternoon rain
using far more words than are actually needed
speaking in a direct way without softening advice
too quiet to be heard over the school intercom
qs.why: Clara explains verbose right after the dash: "you used thirty-four words just to say a storm is coming."

qs.q: Which sentence shows why Owen's first line was not helpful to listeners?
choices: Owen handed his script to his older sister Clara across the kitchen table.
"Writing that the weather will be bad is way too vague because listeners cannot tell whether to grab umbrellas or winter coats."
qs.why: This sentence explains that saying the weather will be bad leaves students unsure whether to bring umbrellas or winter coats.

ev.text: "Writing that the weather will be bad is way too vague because listeners cannot tell whether to grab umbrellas or winter coats."

qs.q: Why does Owen describe the afternoon rain as "moderate" instead of "intense"?
choices: Because he expects steady showers that are neither tiny nor extreme.
Because he wants students to leave their umbrellas at home all day.
Because Clara asked him to remove every mention of rain from the script.
Because a faint mist at sunrise always prevents afternoon storms.
qs.why: Owen contrasts no intense downpours with moderate showers, describing them as "neither a drizzle nor a flood."

qs.q: What is this dialogue mostly about?
choices: A sister warns her brother that reading over the intercom is stressful.
Two siblings argue about whether sixty-two degrees requires a winter coat.
A student improves a weather script by choosing clearer, more exact words.
A meteorologist visits a kitchen to teach students how rainstorms form.
qs.why: With Clara's feedback, Owen replaces vague and wordy phrasing with specific, concise, well-calibrated weather words.

clues.text: you used thirty-four words just to say a storm is coming
weak enough to fade by eight o'clock
neither a drizzle nor a flood
